body:
Replaces the earlier rule that only the session's own program may write state (d-vocab rule 3) — that rule was right about observers and wrong about dispatchers.

A dispatcher is not an observer: it knows when it hands work to a session and when that work returns, so it can write the truth at both ends. Concretely, pi-zmx sets `state=working` before `zmx run`, then `state=done` or `state=failed` on return, and `state=blocked` when it is asking the human to attach and type something (a password prompt is exactly this). The Emacs plugin does the same around its own invocations.

So state means intent, and zmx's own `ended`/`exit_code` means fact: a session can claim working while its task has ended, and the reader shows both without believing either alone. Ordering: blocked, then working, then done/failed, then unknown; absent state is unknown, never idle.

Only one writer is allowed to delete: on attach, a human may clear `state=blocked` because the human arriving is the event that unblocks it. Nothing else writes, and nothing watches.
title: The dispatcher writes state; the reader deletes it honestly
